symptoms: Small red or white pimples on the skin, especially the face
Blackheads (open clogged pores)
Whiteheads (closed clogged pores)
Skin redness and inflammation
Bumps filled with pus or fluid
causes: Overproduction of oil by skin glands
Blocked hair follicles by oil and dead skin cells
Hormonal changes during puberty or stress
Use of certain cosmetics or medications
medical_treatment: Topical creams like benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid help unclog pores
Antibiotics (creams or oral) reduce inflammation and kill bacteria
Retinoid creams to prevent clogged pores
Laser or light therapy targets deep inflammation
Isotretinoin for severe cases (must be used under doctor supervision)
dietary_suggestions: Avoid sugary foods and drinks as they may trigger acne
Limit dairy products which can affect hormone levels
Eat omega-3 rich foods like fish and flaxseeds for skin health
Drink plenty of water to keep skin hydrated
Include zinc-rich foods like pumpkin seeds and lentils to reduce acne
exercise_suggestions: Exercise regularly to improve blood flow and skin health
Wash your face after workouts to remove sweat and bacteria
Avoid tight headgear or helmets that rub against the skin
Do yoga or breathing exercises to manage stress (a known trigger)
Wear clean, breathable clothes during exercise

symptoms: Scaly, rough patches on sun-exposed areas of the skin
Sores that don’t heal or keep returning
Firm, skin-colored or reddish lumps
Crusting or bleeding spots
Lesions with irregular borders or color changes
causes: Prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays from sunlight
Weakened immune system due to disease or medication
Older age and fair skin type
medical_treatment: Cryotherapy (freezing the lesion with liquid nitrogen)
Topical chemotherapy creams to destroy abnormal cells
Minor surgery to remove cancerous tissue
Laser treatment for precision removal
Photodynamic therapy using light-activated drugs to kill abnormal cells
dietary_suggestions: Eat foods rich in antioxidants (like berries, spinach) to protect skin cells
Avoid processed meats and high-fat foods
Increase vitamin D intake (consult doctor if sun exposure is limited)
Include citrus fruits and leafy greens for immune support
Drink green tea, which may help in skin cell repair
exercise_suggestions: Engage in light indoor exercises like stretching or walking
Wear protective clothing and sunscreen when exercising outdoors
Avoid sun exposure between 10 AM and 4 PM
Stay hydrated during physical activity
Try mindfulness-based exercises like Tai Chi or yoga to reduce stress

symptoms: Dry and itchy skin that worsens at night
Red or brownish patches on hands, feet, face, or neck
Thickened, cracked, or scaly skin
Oozing and crusting after scratching
Raw, sensitive skin from frequent rubbing
causes: Genetics (family history of eczema or allergies)
Exposure to irritants like soaps or chemicals
Allergens like dust, pollen, or pet dander
medical_treatment: Moisturizers (emollients) applied several times daily to lock in moisture
Topical steroid creams to reduce inflammation
Antihistamines to reduce itching and help sleep
Phototherapy (light therapy) for chronic cases
Prescription creams that modulate the immune response (like tacrolimus)
dietary_suggestions: Avoid trigger foods (e.g., dairy, eggs, gluten) if known
Eat foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids to reduce inflammation
Include fruits and vegetables for skin-supporting vitamins
Drink lots of water to maintain hydration
Consume probiotic-rich foods like yogurt for gut health
exercise_suggestions: Do moderate exercise like walking or cycling
Shower immediately after sweating to prevent irritation
Wear soft, breathable clothing during workouts
Avoid overheating or hot environments
Try stress-relieving activities like swimming or yoga

symptoms: Large, fluid-filled blisters on the skin
Red, itchy, or painful skin before blister formation
Skin peeling or raw areas after blisters burst
Blisters inside the mouth or mucous membranes
Delayed wound healing
causes: Autoimmune disorders where the body attacks healthy skin
medical_treatment: Corticosteroid creams or pills to reduce immune attacks
Immune-suppressing drugs to stop blister formation
Wound care with sterile dressings to prevent infection
Antibiotics for infected blisters
Special oral medications for severe or resistant cases
dietary_suggestions: Eat soft, easy-to-chew foods if mouth blisters are present
Avoid spicy or acidic foods that may irritate blisters
Stay hydrated to support skin repair
Consume foods rich in vitamins A, C, and E
Avoid foods known to trigger flare-ups
exercise_suggestions: Do gentle movements like walking or light yoga
Avoid friction on skin to prevent new blisters
Wear loose, soft clothing during exercise
Use cooling fans or AC to prevent sweating
Stretch at home instead of going to gyms with high contact

Fair skin with freckles and light hair

Targeted drugs for specific genetic mutations
Radiation therapy in advanced cases
Regular skin check-ups after treatment

Include foods rich in vitamin D (if safe to do so)
Avoid charred meats and processed foods
Drink green tea for skin-protective benefits
Stay well hydrated throughout the day

Wear sun-protective clothing during outdoor workouts
Avoid sun exposure between 10 AM and 4 PM
Choose indoor or shaded environments for activities
Practice stress management techniques like meditation
